readerTitle: Ten thousand customers and no network effect
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, 지역 기술자 소개 모임, 메모 앱) + 일반적 관찰 (전화기, 팩스)
insight: 네트워크 효과는 고객 수가 아니라, 새 고객 한 명이 기존 고객에게 주는 가치로 판단한다.
misconception: 고객이 많고 빠르게 늘면 네트워크 효과가 있다. 규모의 경제나 입소문도 네트워크 효과다.

sources.text: Katz, M. & Shapiro, C. (1985). Network Externalities, Competition, and Compatibility. American Economic Review.
전화기·팩스 예시는 네트워크 효과를 설명할 때 널리 쓰이는 일반적 관찰
청소 서비스, 기술자 소개 모임, 메모 앱은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 전화기·팩스 예시는 특정 수치 없이 원리만 설명했습니다. 역사적 사실 주장은 넣지 않았습니다.
Katz & Shapiro(1985) 서지 정보(학술지명, 연도)를 게시 전에 확인하세요.
청소 회사 고객 수 10,000은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 다른 실제 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Ten thousand customers and no network effect
body: A house-cleaning company has grown to 10,000 households in two years. Its pitch deck says: "Every new customer makes us stronger. That's our network effect."
It sounds convincing. Growth is real, and customers like the service. But the claim fails a simple test, and the test is worth knowing for your own business.

image.label: Cleaning van in front of many houses
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 청소 서비스 밴 한 대와 그 뒤로 길게 늘어선 집들. 집들 사이에 연결선이 전혀 없다는 점이 눈에 띄게. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: An investor asks: do you have a network effect?
body: You run that cleaning company. An investor wants an honest answer before she commits. Which one do you give?

options.text: Yes. More customers means more reviews, so people trust us more
options.feedback: Reviews do help you win new customers. But a stranger's review doesn't make your cleaner do a better job for the customers you already have.

options.text: Yes. More customers in one area means shorter drives and lower costs
options.feedback: That's a real advantage, called economies of scale. A well-funded rival can buy the same density, so it protects you less than a true network effect.

options.text: Not really. A new customer doesn't make the service better for existing ones
options.feedback: Honest, and it's the right test. You lose a buzzword but gain the investor's trust, and a clearer view of what really protects you.

cards.title: Does the neighbor's sign-up help Mrs. Lee?
body: Picture one long-time customer. Her neighbor signs up. Is her own cleaning any better? No. It's the same cleaner, the same checklist, the same price.
In busy weeks, it may even get worse. More households compete for the same Saturday slots.
Now picture a phone. When her neighbor gets one, Mrs. Lee's phone becomes more useful. She has one more person she can call. That difference is the whole idea.

cards.title: Direct network effects
body: A **direct network effect** happens when each new user makes the product more valuable to other users of the same kind.
The value lives in the connections between users, not in the product itself. One fax machine is useless. Two can send messages. A thousand form a network everyone wants to join.
A quick check: would the product be worth much to a single user alone? If not, you're probably looking at a direct network effect.

image.label: One phone alone vs many phones linked
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에는 전화기 한 대만 덩그러니 있고 "Worth little" 라벨. 오른쪽에는 전화기 여러 대가 선으로 촘촘히 연결되고 "Worth more with every new line" 라벨. 실제 브랜드 표시 없음.

cards.title: Three things that feel like network effects but aren't.
body: Each of these helps a growing business. None makes the product better for existing customers just because someone new joined.
list: **Scale:** costs fall as you grow. Useful, but money can copy it.
**Popularity:** people trust what others use. That wins new customers, not better service.
**Brand:** a known name lowers the risk of trying you.
cards.callout: Real network effects are harder to copy, because the value sits in who is already there.

cards.title: The same trade, a different model.
body: Now imagine a local group of electricians, plumbers and painters who pass jobs to each other. A plumber finds bad wiring and calls a member electrician.
Here, each new member does help existing members. One more trade means more referrals flowing to everyone. Leaving the group means losing that flow.
Same industry as the cleaning company, very different economics. Network effects come from how a business is built, not from the sector it's in.

cards.title: User counts can mislead.
body: A network with a million members means little if the people you need aren't in it. What matters is how many of *your* contacts, partners or teammates use it.
And more users isn't always better. Past a point, crowding, noise and spam can lower the value for everyone. Later lessons cover when networks get worse.

cards.title: Now it's a note-taking app.
body: Your note-taking app has steady growth, but each user mostly writes alone. Your team wants a real direct network effect. Which move would create one?

options.text: Shared workspaces where teammates edit, comment and link notes together
options.feedback: Now each new teammate makes the app more useful for the rest of the team. The cost: shared features are harder to build and to get right.

options.text: Cut prices as server costs fall with scale
options.feedback: Cheaper is nice, but it's scale, not a network. A rival with more funding can match it, and users still have no reason to stay for each other.

options.text: Show a "Trusted by millions" badge on the sign-up page
options.feedback: Social proof may lift sign-ups. It doesn't change the value of the app for anyone already using it.

cards.softwareNote: In software, direct network effects usually come from features that connect users of the same kind: messaging, shared files, multiplayer play, or a common format others must use to work with you.

cards.title: Ask whether the next customer makes it better for the last one.
body: If a new customer adds value for the ones you already have, you have a direct network effect. If not, your strengths are elsewhere, and that's fine to say.
**Try it today:** pick one long-time customer. Write down what changes for them when your next customer joins.
